items.c: Salt, sugar, sex from outside in: glomerulosa aldosterone, fasciculata cortisol, reticularis androgens, medulla catecholamines.
items.a: Layers of the adrenal gland from outside in: capsule, zona glomerulosa making aldosterone, zona fasciculata making cortisol, zona reticularis making androgens, and the medulla making adrenaline and noradrenaline.
items.rn: Adrenal cortex and medulla

items.c: Renin, ACE, AT1: angiotensin II constricts vessels and releases aldosterone, which keeps sodium and water and wastes potassium.
items.a: Flow diagram of the renin angiotensin aldosterone system: low renal perfusion or low sodium at the macula densa or sympathetic activity releases renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, ACE converts it to angiotensin II, which constricts vessels and drives aldosterone, retaining sodium and water.
items.rn: Adrenal cortex and medulla

items.c: Stress to CRH to ACTH to cortisol, with cortisol shutting off its own drive; steroid therapy suppresses the axis.
items.a: Hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis: stress releases CRH from the hypothalamus, which releases ACTH from the anterior pituitary, which stimulates cortisol from the zona fasciculata; cortisol feeds back negatively on both CRH and ACTH.
items.rn: Adrenal cortex and medulla

items.c: Tyrosine hydroxylase is rate limiting; PNMT needs cortisol, so adrenaline is made mainly in the adrenal medulla.
items.a: Catecholamine synthesis in order: tyrosine to L-DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate limiting step, then to dopamine, noradrenaline, and adrenaline by PNMT, which is induced by cortisol.
items.rn: Adrenal cortex and medulla

items.t: Autonomic nervous system, hypothalamic nuclei and pupillary reflexes
items.c: Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. Location of the lesion decides whether the face sweats.
items.a: Three neuron sympathetic pathway to the eye: first order from posterior hypothalamus to the ciliospinal centre at C8 to T2, second order through the sympathetic chain over the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion, third order along the carotid to the pupil dilator and tarsal muscle; interruption gives Horner syndrome.
items.rn: Autonomic nervous system, hypothalamic nuclei and pupillary reflexes

items.c: Sympathetic: thoracolumbar, short pre, long post, noradrenaline. Parasympathetic: craniosacral, long pre, short post, acetylcholine.
items.a: Two column comparison of sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow: sympathetic from T1 to L2 with short preganglionic fibres and long noradrenergic postganglionic fibres, parasympathetic from cranial nerves III VII IX X and S2 to S4 with long preganglionic fibres and short cholinergic postganglionic fibres.
items.rn: Autonomic nervous system

items.c: Gq: alpha-1 and M3 (constrict, secrete). Gs: beta-1 and beta-2 (heart, relax). Gi: M2 and alpha-2.
items.a: Table of autonomic receptors with G protein pathway and effects: alpha-1 Gq vasoconstriction, alpha-2 Gi, beta-1 Gs raising heart rate, beta-2 Gs relaxing bronchi, M2 Gi slowing the heart, M3 Gq contracting gut and glands, nicotinic ganglionic and muscle channels.
items.rn: Autonomic nervous system

items.c: Rising pressure fires baroreceptors, which brake the heart through the vagus and relax vessels; standing does the opposite.
items.a: Baroreceptor reflex loop: raised blood pressure stretches carotid sinus and aortic arch receptors, afferents via IX and X reach the nucleus tractus solitarius, which increases vagal tone and reduces sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate and vessel tone and so pressure.
items.rn: Autonomic nervous system

items.c: Spinal cord injury at or above T6: noxious stimulus below the lesion leads to severe hypertension; sit up and remove the trigger.
items.a: Autonomic dysreflexia in spinal injury above T6: a stimulus below the lesion, usually a full bladder or bowel, causes a sympathetic surge with severe hypertension; baroreflex slows the heart but cannot relax vessels below the lesion; treat by sitting up, removing the stimulus and lowering the pressure.
items.rn: Autonomic nervous system

items.t: Blood groups and transfusion: ABO, Rh and reactions
items.c: O has no antigens (universal red cell donor); AB has no antibodies (universal recipient).
items.a: Table of ABO groups with red cell antigen, plasma antibody and which red cells each can receive: A gets A and O, B gets B and O, AB gets all, O gets only O.
items.rn: Blood groups and transfusion: ABO, Rh and reactions

items.t: Blood groups and transfusion: ABO, Rh and reactions
items.c: Anti-D given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of a sensitising event prevents the mother making her own antibody.
items.a: Sequence of haemolytic disease of the newborn: an RhD negative mother is sensitised by fetomaternal bleeding at delivery or a sensitising event, makes anti-D IgG, and in a later RhD positive pregnancy the antibody crosses the placenta causing haemolysis; anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitisation.
items.rn: Blood groups and transfusion: ABO, Rh and reactions

items.t: Blood groups and transfusion: ABO, Rh and reactions
items.c: Major crossmatch protects the recipient and is the one that matters; in an emergency use group O negative.
items.a: Comparison of major and minor crossmatch: major crossmatch mixes donor red cells with recipient serum to detect recipient antibodies to donor cells, minor crossmatch mixes donor serum with recipient cells; emergency uses O negative red cells.
items.rn: Blood groups and transfusion: ABO, Rh and reactions

items.c: 60-40-20 rule: TBW is 60% (D2O), ICF is 40% (calculated), ECF is 20% (Inulin), divided into interstitial fluid 15% and plasma 5% (Evans blue).
items.a: The 60-40-20 rule for total body water distribution in a 70 kg individual showing intracellular fluid, interstitial fluid, plasma, and their respective dilution volume measurement markers.
items.rn: Body fluid compartments and homeostasis

items.t: Regulation of blood pressure: reflexes and hormonal control
items.c: Baroreceptor reflex pathway from carotid sinus and aortic arch to the brainstem.
items.a: Anatomical diagram of the arterial baroreceptor reflex showing stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch signalling via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the nucleus tractus solitarius and vasomotor centre in the brainstem.
items.rn: Regulation of blood pressure: reflexes and hormonal control

items.t: Regulation of blood pressure: reflexes and hormonal control
items.c: Between about 60 and 160 mmHg the organ holds flow steady; chronic hypertension shifts the plateau to the right.
items.a: Plot of organ blood flow against mean arterial pressure showing an autoregulatory plateau between about 60 and 160 mmHg, with flow falling below and rising above, and a dashed curve shifted right by sympathetic vasoconstriction.
items.rn: Regulation of blood pressure: reflexes and hormonal control

items.c: PTH and calcitriol raise calcium; calcitonin lowers it weakly. PTH wastes phosphate.
items.a: Feedback loop of calcium control: low plasma calcium raises PTH, which increases bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, phosphate excretion and activation of vitamin D to calcitriol, which increases gut calcium absorption; high calcium switches PTH off and calcitonin opposes.
items.rn: Calcium and bone metabolism

items.c: Osteoblasts control osteoclasts through RANKL; OPG blocks it; denosumab is an antibody against RANKL.
items.a: RANKL pathway of bone remodelling: osteoblasts express RANKL that binds RANK on osteoclast precursors, driving osteoclast formation and resorption; osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL; osteoblasts then lay down new bone.
items.rn: Calcium and bone metabolism

items.c: Stones, bones, groans, moans. Fluids first, then a bisphosphonate.
items.a: Table of causes and features of hypercalcaemia: primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy are the commonest causes, with stones, bones, groans and psychic moans, and first line treatment with saline then bisphosphonate.
items.rn: Calcium and bone metabolism

items.c: Chvostek: tap the facial nerve, the cheek twitches. Trousseau: cuff inflation causes carpal spasm.
items.a: Table of causes and signs of hypocalcaemia: hypoparathyroidism after thyroid surgery, DiGeorge syndrome, pseudohypoparathyroidism, with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, perioral tingling and tetany.
items.rn: Calcium and bone metabolism

items.c: Phases in order: atrial systole, isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, diastasis.
items.a: Wiggers diagram of one cardiac cycle with left ventricular, aortic and left atrial pressure, ventricular volume, ECG and heart sounds, marked with mitral valve closure, aortic valve opening, aortic valve closure with the dicrotic notch, and mitral valve opening.
items.rn: Cardiac cycle and cardiac output

items.c: First and second heart sounds correlated with atrioventricular and semilunar valves.
items.a: Cardiac valve and phonocardiogram diagram showing the first heart sound (S1) from mitral and tricuspid valve closure at the start of ventricular systole and the second heart sound (S2) from aortic and pulmonary valve closure.
items.rn: Cardiac cycle and cardiac output

items.c: Same filling, more output with a positive inotrope; in failure the curve flattens and output falls.
items.a: Frank-Starling curves of stroke volume against end-diastolic volume: normal curve rising then flattening, a higher steeper curve with increased contractility, and a flatter curve in heart failure.
items.rn: Cardiac cycle and cardiac output

items.t: Cardiac electrophysiology, action potentials and pacemaker automatism
items.c: Pacemaker cells drift up by the funny current; ventricular cells snap up with sodium and plateau with calcium.
items.a: Overlaid action potentials of a sinoatrial node cell and a ventricular myocyte: the node has no stable resting potential and drifts upward in phase 4 until a slow calcium upstroke, the ventricle rests at minus 90, fires rapidly through sodium channels and holds a calcium plateau.
items.rn: Cardiac electrophysiology, action potentials and pacemaker automatism

items.t: Cardiac electrophysiology, action potentials and pacemaker automatism
items.c: Comparative waveform schematics of working ventricular myocyte action potential phases and sinoatrial nodal pacemaker prepotentials.
items.a: Cardiac ventricular and pacemaker action potentials
items.rn: Cardiac electrophysiology, action potentials and pacemaker automatism

items.c: Purkinje cells are the sole cortical output and are inhibitory; mossy fibres carry context, climbing fibres carry errors.
items.a: Circuit of the cerebellar cortex: cortex through pontine nuclei sends mossy fibres to granule cells, parallel fibres excite Purkinje cells; climbing fibres from the inferior olive also excite Purkinje cells; Purkinje cells inhibit deep cerebellar nuclei, the only output.
items.rn: Cerebellum and basal ganglia function

items.c: TRAP: Tremor at rest, Rigidity, Akinesia, Postural instability; the cause is nigral dopamine loss.
items.a: Parkinson disease circuit: loss of substantia nigra dopamine weakens the direct pathway and releases the indirect pathway, so globus pallidus internus over-inhibits the thalamus, causing bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor.
items.rn: Cerebellum and basal ganglia function

items.c: Hemiballismus: subthalamic nucleus stroke. Huntington: caudate loss and CAG expansion.
items.a: Table of hyperkinetic movement disorders by lesion: Huntington caudate and putamen with CAG repeat, hemiballismus contralateral subthalamic nucleus, Sydenham chorea after streptococcal infection, Wilson disease copper in basal ganglia, tardive dyskinesia from dopamine blockers.
items.rn: Cerebellum and basal ganglia function

items.t: Countercurrent mechanism, medullary gradient and ADH regulation
items.c: Vasa recta are countercurrent exchangers: they carry away water and solute without washing out the medullary gradient.
items.a: Schematic of the vasa recta hairpin beside a medullary osmotic gradient from 300 at the cortex to 1200 mOsm per kg at the papilla: the descending limb gains solute and loses water, the ascending limb loses solute and gains water, so the gradient is preserved.
items.rn: Countercurrent mechanism, medullary gradient and ADH regulation

items.t: Countercurrent mechanism, medullary gradient and ADH regulation
items.c: Longitudinal cross-section of renal cortex and medulla illustrating loop of Henle countercurrent multiplier, vasa recta exchanger and ADH water reabsorption.
items.a: Renal medullary countercurrent multiplier schematic
items.rn: Countercurrent mechanism, medullary gradient and ADH regulation

items.t: Digestion and absorption: enzymes, bile and malabsorption
items.c: Each site digests a different macronutrient; the brush border completes it.
items.a: Table of digestive secretions by site with enzymes and substrates: salivary amylase and lingual lipase in the mouth, acid pepsin and intrinsic factor in the stomach, pancreatic trypsin amylase and lipase in the duodenum, brush border disaccharidases and peptidases.
items.rn: Digestion and absorption: enzymes, bile and malabsorption

items.t: Digestion and absorption: enzymes, bile and malabsorption
items.c: Bile acids are recycled: ileal reabsorption returns most of the pool to the liver. Ileal disease causes bile acid malabsorption.
items.a: Enterohepatic circulation of bile acids: liver makes bile, gallbladder stores it, cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder to release it into the duodenum, bile acids form micelles with fat, and about 95 percent is reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver by the portal vein.
items.rn: Digestion and absorption: enzymes, bile and malabsorption

items.t: Digestion and absorption: enzymes, bile and malabsorption
items.c: Glucose and galactose ride sodium (SGLT1); fructose uses GLUT5; all leave by GLUT2; the Na+/K+ ATPase drives it all.
items.a: Enterocyte schematic: SGLT1 brings glucose and galactose in with sodium, GLUT5 brings fructose in, PepT1 brings small peptides with hydrogen, GLUT2 releases all three sugars at the basolateral side, and the sodium potassium pump powers the sodium gradient.
items.rn: Digestion and absorption: enzymes, bile and malabsorption

items.t: Female reproductive physiology and menstrual cycle
items.c: FSH recruits and selects the dominant follicle; the LH surge ovulates; the corpus luteum sustains progesterone for about two weeks.
items.a: Stages of follicle development: primordial, primary, secondary, antral, Graafian follicle, ovulation under the LH surge, corpus luteum making progesterone, and corpus albicans if no pregnancy.
items.rn: Female reproductive physiology and menstrual cycle

items.t: Female reproductive physiology and menstrual cycle
items.c: Oestradiol peak triggers the LH surge; LH surge ovulates; progesterone dominates the luteal phase.
items.a: Plot of the 28 day menstrual cycle with FSH, LH, oestradiol and progesterone: FSH rises early, oestradiol peaks before ovulation, an LH surge on day 14 triggers ovulation, progesterone peaks in the luteal phase; follicular and luteal phases and the proliferative and secretory endometrium are labelled.
items.rn: Female reproductive physiology and menstrual cycle

items.t: Female reproductive physiology and menstrual cycle
items.c: hCG peaks at 8 to 10 weeks and then falls; the placenta takes over progesterone from the corpus luteum around weeks 7 to 9.
items.a: Plot of hormone levels across pregnancy: hCG rises from implantation to a peak at about 8 to 10 weeks then falls to a plateau, progesterone shifts from corpus luteum to placenta around weeks 7 to 9 and keeps rising, oestriol rises steadily to term.
items.rn: Female reproductive physiology and menstrual cycle

items.t: Gas exchange, ventilation-perfusion matching and pulmonary circulation
items.c: Normal A-a gradient is under about 15 mmHg; hypoventilation lowers PaO2 with a normal gradient.
items.a: Worked alveolar gas equation at sea level: inspired PO2 150 mmHg minus PaCO2 40 divided by respiratory quotient 0.8 gives alveolar PO2 100, minus arterial PO2 about 90 gives an A-a gradient of about 10 mmHg; widening points to V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion defect.
items.rn: Gas exchange, ventilation-perfusion matching and pulmonary circulation

items.c: Right shift (acid, CO2, heat, 2,3-BPG) unloads oxygen; left shift and carbon monoxide trap it, so tissues are starved even at normal PaO2.
items.a: Oxygen haemoglobin dissociation curves: normal sigmoid curve with P50 of 26.6 mmHg, a right shifted curve with easier oxygen release, a left shifted curve with tighter binding, and a carbon monoxide curve that is both left shifted and lowered; arterial and venous points marked.
items.rn: Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport

items.t: Renal blood flow and glomerular filtration
items.c: Three layers: fenestrated endothelium, charged basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragm. Loss of charge gives albuminuria.
items.a: Cross-section of the glomerular filtration barrier from capillary lumen to urinary space: fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane with negative charge, and podocyte foot processes joined by slit diaphragms; water and small solutes pass, albumin is held back by size and charge.
items.rn: Renal blood flow and glomerular filtration

items.c: GH acts mostly through IGF-1; IGF-1 is the stable screening test for excess or deficiency.
items.a: Growth hormone axis: GHRH raises and somatostatin lowers growth hormone from the anterior pituitary; growth hormone stimulates IGF-1 from the liver, which acts on bone and tissues and feeds back to suppress growth hormone.
items.rn: Growth, puberty and ageing physiology

items.c: Puberty starts when GnRH pulses wake up; the first sign is breast budding in girls and testicular enlargement in boys.
items.a: Hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis at puberty: pulsatile GnRH from the hypothalamus drives LH and FSH, which act on the gonads to make sex steroids and gametes, which cause secondary sexual characteristics; feedback is negative before puberty and set to allow cyclic surges in females.
items.rn: Growth, puberty and ageing physiology

items.t: Haemodynamics and microcirculation: core principles for exams
items.c: Turbulence is noisy: it causes murmurs and bruits where narrowing raises velocity.
items.a: Two tubes: laminar flow with parallel streamlines and a parabolic velocity profile, and turbulent flow with chaotic eddies that happens when the Reynolds number exceeds about 2000, with the Reynolds number formula.
items.rn: Haemodynamics and microcirculation: core principles for exams

items.c: Adhesion (vWF, GPIb), activation (ADP, TXA2), aggregation (GPIIb/IIIa, fibrinogen); each step has a drug.
items.a: Primary haemostasis: vascular spasm, platelet adhesion by von Willebrand factor binding GPIb to collagen, activation releasing ADP and thromboxane A2, aggregation through GPIIb IIIa and fibrinogen; aspirin blocks thromboxane, clopidogrel blocks the ADP receptor, abciximab blocks GPIIb IIIa.
items.rn: Haemostasis: platelets, cascades and fibrinolysis

items.c: PT follows the extrinsic pathway (VII) and warfarin; APTT follows the intrinsic pathway and heparin.
items.a: Coagulation cascade: intrinsic pathway XII XI IX with VIII and extrinsic pathway tissue factor with VIIa both activate X, which with V converts prothrombin to thrombin, converting fibrinogen to fibrin, cross linked by XIII; PT tests the extrinsic route, APTT the intrinsic, and warfarin lowers II VII IX and X.
items.rn: Haemostasis: platelets, cascades and fibrinolysis

items.c: D-dimer rises when cross-linked fibrin has been broken down: it flags clot formation and lysis.
items.a: Fibrinolysis: tissue plasminogen activator converts plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin into fibrin degradation products including D-dimer; PAI-1 and alpha-2 antiplasmin inhibit it, and tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen binding.
items.rn: Haemostasis: platelets, cascades and fibrinolysis

items.t: Hearing and vestibular function: high-yield physiology
items.c: Area ratio times lever ratio gives about 22 times pressure gain; without it most sound would reflect from the cochlear fluid.
items.a: Impedance matching of the middle ear: the large tympanic membrane area focuses force on the small oval window, about a 17 fold area gain, the ossicular lever adds about 1.3, giving roughly 22 fold pressure gain that overcomes air to fluid reflection of sound.
items.rn: Hearing and vestibular function: high-yield physiology

items.t: Sleep, EEG, Learning, Memory and Speech
items.c: Left: language and Gerstmann tetrad. Right: spatial neglect, face recognition, awareness of illness.
items.a: Table of hemisphere syndromes: dominant left hemisphere aphasia and Gerstmann syndrome with agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left right confusion; non-dominant right hemisphere neglect, anosognosia, prosopagnosia and constructional apraxia.
items.rn: Sleep, EEG, Learning, Memory and Speech

items.c: Peptides use surface receptors and second messengers; steroids and thyroid hormone enter the cell and act on DNA.
items.a: Table of hormone receptor classes: peptide hormones bind surface G protein receptors using cAMP or IP3 and calcium, insulin and IGF-1 use tyrosine kinase, growth hormone and prolactin use JAK STAT, steroid and thyroid hormones use nuclear receptors that change gene transcription.
items.rn: Hormone action, hypothalamus and pituitary

items.c: Prolactin is the only anterior pituitary hormone under dominant inhibition; cutting the stalk raises it.
items.a: Control of prolactin: hypothalamic dopamine tonically inhibits lactotrophs through D2 receptors; TRH, oestrogen and the suckling reflex stimulate release; prolactin drives milk synthesis and suppresses GnRH.
items.rn: Hormone action, hypothalamus and pituitary

items.c: Each axis is hypothalamic releasing hormone, pituitary hormone, then a target gland hormone with negative feedback.
items.a: Table of hypothalamic pituitary axes: GHRH to growth hormone to IGF-1, TRH to TSH to thyroid hormones, CRH to ACTH to cortisol, GnRH to LH and FSH to sex steroids, dopamine inhibiting prolactin.
items.rn: Hormone action, hypothalamus and pituitary

items.c: Appetite regulation: Lateral hypothalamus drives feeding (orexin/ghrelin); Ventromedial nucleus mediates satiety (leptin/alpha-MSH).
items.a: Schematic of hypothalamic appetite centers showing the lateral hunger center, ventromedial satiety center, and arcuate nucleus integrating peripheral hormonal signals including leptin, ghrelin, insulin, and orexin.
items.rn: Hypothalamus, limbic system and thermoregulation

items.c: Circadian pathway from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus and pineal gland.
items.a: Mid-sagittal view of the brain showing light input from the retina reaching the suprachiasmatic nucleus above the optic chiasm and regulating melatonin release from the pineal gland.
items.rn: Hypothalamus, limbic system and thermoregulation

items.t: Hypoxia, high altitude and environmental physiology
items.c: Only hypoxic hypoxia has a low PaO2; the other three have normal PaO2, so pulse oximetry can mislead.
items.a: Table of four hypoxia types: hypoxic with low PaO2 such as altitude, anaemic with normal PaO2 but low oxygen content, stagnant with normal PaO2 and low flow as in shock, histotoxic with normal PaO2 where cells cannot use oxygen as in cyanide poisoning.
items.rn: Hypoxia, high altitude and environmental physiology

items.t: Hypoxia, high altitude and environmental physiology
items.c: Descent is definitive for all three; acetazolamide prevents AMS, dexamethasone treats HACE, nifedipine treats HAPE.
items.a: Table of high altitude illness: acute mountain sickness with headache and nausea treated by rest and acetazolamide, high altitude cerebral oedema with ataxia and confusion treated by descent and dexamethasone, high altitude pulmonary oedema with dyspnoea and crackles treated by descent and nifedipine.
items.rn: Hypoxia, high altitude and environmental physiology

items.t: Hypoxia, high altitude and environmental physiology
items.c: Pressure adds one atmosphere per 10 m; air in the lungs and sinuses halves at 10 m, which drives barotrauma and bubble formation on ascent.
items.a: Plot of absolute pressure and relative gas volume against diving depth: pressure rises by one atmosphere per 10 metres of sea water, so a gas volume halves at 10 metres and falls to a quarter at 30 metres, following Boyle law.
items.rn: Hypoxia, high altitude and environmental physiology

items.c: LH to Leydig to testosterone; FSH to Sertoli to sperm and inhibin B.
items.a: Male hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis: GnRH drives LH and FSH; LH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone, FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and inhibin B; testosterone feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary and inhibin B on FSH.
items.rn: Male reproductive physiology

items.c: Testosterone builds muscle and red cells; DHT makes the external genitalia, prostate and hair; hypogonadism reverses these.
items.a: Table of testosterone sources and actions: made by Leydig cells from cholesterol under LH, converted to DHT in the prostate and skin by 5-alpha reductase, causing male external genitalia, prostate growth and hair, with anabolic effects on muscle and bone, erythropoiesis and libido.
items.rn: Male reproductive physiology

items.c: Parasympathetic: point (erection). Sympathetic: shoot (emission). PDE5 inhibitors need nitric oxide, so nitrates are forbidden.
items.a: Neural control of erection and ejaculation: parasympathetic S2 to S4 nerves release nitric oxide raising cGMP and relaxing corporal smooth muscle for erection; PDE5 inhibitors prolong cGMP; sympathetic T11 to L2 drives emission and somatic pudendal fibres drive ejaculation.
items.rn: Male reproductive physiology

items.c: Azoospermia means no sperm: obstructive (normal FSH, normal testes) or non-obstructive (high FSH, small testes).
items.a: Table of normal semen parameters from World Health Organization lower reference limits: volume 1.5 mL, concentration 15 million per mL, total motility 40 percent, progressive motility 32 percent, normal forms 4 percent by strict criteria.
items.rn: Male reproductive physiology

items.t: Mechanics of breathing, lung compliance and airway resistance
items.c: Laplace: P = 2T/r. Surfactant lowers surface tension, more so in small alveoli, preventing collapse; premature infants lack it.
items.a: Two connected alveoli of different size: by the law of Laplace pressure equals two times surface tension divided by radius, so without surfactant the small alveolus has higher pressure and would empty into the large one; surfactant lowers tension more in the small alveolus and equalises pressure.
items.rn: Mechanics of breathing, lung compliance and airway resistance

items.t: Mechanics of breathing, lung compliance and airway resistance
items.c: Cross-section of terminal respiratory units illustrating alveolar surface tension forces, surfactant distribution and airway resistance profiles.
items.a: Pulmonary mechanics and surfactant dynamics
items.rn: Mechanics of breathing, lung compliance and airway resistance

items.t: Resting membrane potential and action potential
items.c: Sodium influx drives the upstroke; potassium efflux drives repolarisation and the undershoot.
items.a: Plot of one neuronal action potential against time: resting at minus 70 millivolts, threshold at minus 55, rapid depolarisation to about plus 35 as sodium channels open, repolarisation as potassium channels open, undershoot below rest, and return to rest.
items.rn: Resting membrane potential and action potential

items.t: Resting membrane potential and action potential
items.c: Graded potentials decay with distance; action potentials do not.
items.a: Plot of response amplitude against distance: a graded electrotonic potential decays exponentially with distance, while an action potential regenerates and keeps a constant amplitude along the axon.
items.rn: Resting membrane potential and action potential

items.t: Cell membrane and transport: the essentials
items.c: Passive goes downhill without ATP; primary active uses ATP directly; secondary active borrows energy from the sodium gradient.
items.a: Table of membrane transport mechanisms: simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion via channels or carriers, primary active transport using ATP such as the sodium potassium pump, and secondary active transport driven by the sodium gradient such as SGLT.
items.rn: Cell membrane and transport: the essentials

items.t: Cell membrane and transport: the essentials
items.c: Carrier-mediated transport saturates (Tmax); simple diffusion never does.
items.a: Plot of transport rate against concentration gradient: simple diffusion is a straight rising line, facilitated diffusion rises and saturates at a transport maximum, showing carrier specificity, saturation and competition.
items.rn: Cell membrane and transport: the essentials

items.c: NGAL and KIM-1 rise within hours of tubular injury, earlier than creatinine.
items.a: Table of kidney injury biomarkers: cystatin C freely filtered marker of GFR, NGAL early marker of acute kidney injury from tubular injury, KIM-1 marker of proximal tubular damage, IL-18 inflammatory marker in acute tubular necrosis.
items.rn: Mixed practice: physiology rapid review

items.c: Endothelium makes NO, smooth muscle responds with cGMP: nitrates, sildenafil and endothelium-dependent relaxation all share this pathway.
items.a: Nitric oxide signalling: endothelial nitric oxide synthase makes nitric oxide from arginine, which diffuses into smooth muscle, activates guanylyl cyclase to raise cGMP and relaxes the muscle; nitrates donate nitric oxide and PDE5 inhibitors prolong cGMP.
items.rn: Mixed practice: physiology rapid review

items.c: Indomethacin closes a PDA; prostaglandin E1 keeps the duct open in duct-dependent heart disease.
items.a: Why the ductus arteriosus is open before birth: prostaglandin E2 and E1 acting on EP4 receptors and low fetal oxygen keep it dilated; after birth oxygen rises and prostaglandins fall so it constricts; indomethacin closes a patent duct and alprostadil keeps it open when needed.
items.rn: Mixed practice: physiology rapid review

items.t: GI motility: swallowing, gastric emptying and defecation
items.c: Only the oral phase is voluntary; achalasia is failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax.
items.a: Flow diagram of swallowing: voluntary oral phase pushes the bolus back, involuntary pharyngeal phase raises the soft palate and larynx and tilts the epiglottis while the upper oesophageal sphincter relaxes, then oesophageal peristalsis moves the bolus and the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes.
items.rn: GI motility: swallowing, gastric emptying and defecation

items.t: Spinal reflexes, motor control and posture
items.c: Muscle spindle anatomy with intrafusal fibres, Ia/II afferents and gamma motor supply.
items.a: Cutaway anatomical illustration of a skeletal muscle spindle lying in parallel with extrafusal muscle fibres, showing nuclear bag and nuclear chain intrafusal fibres, Ia and II sensory afferents, and gamma motor neuron endings.
items.rn: Spinal reflexes, motor control and posture

items.t: Spinal reflexes, motor control and posture
items.c: Monosynaptic stretch reflex: muscle spindle Ia afferent synapses directly on alpha motor neuron, with reciprocal interneuron inhibition of antagonist.
items.a: Neuroanatomical circuit diagram showing the muscle spindle Ia primary sensory afferent synapsing directly onto the alpha motor neuron in the spinal cord ventral horn, alongside reciprocal inhibition of antagonist muscles.
items.rn: Spinal reflexes, motor control and posture

items.t: Spinal reflexes, motor control and posture
items.c: Golgi tendon organ in series with muscle mediating the inverse stretch reflex.
items.a: Anatomical and physiological diagram of the inverse stretch reflex showing the Golgi tendon organ in series with skeletal muscle sending Ib afferent fibres to an inhibitory spinal interneuron that inhibits the alpha motor neuron.
items.rn: Spinal reflexes, motor control and posture

items.t: Nerve fibre classification, conduction and degeneration
items.c: Larger and myelinated means faster. A delta is fast sharp pain; C is slow dull pain.
items.a: Table of Erlanger Gasser nerve fibre types with diameter, conduction velocity and function: A alpha proprioception and motor, A beta touch, A gamma muscle spindle motor, A delta fast pain and cold, B preganglionic autonomic, C slow pain and postganglionic sympathetic.
items.rn: Nerve fibre classification, conduction and degeneration

items.t: Nerve fibre classification, conduction and degeneration
items.c: Myelinated nerve fibre showing nodes of Ranvier and clefts of Schmidt-Lantermann.
items.a: Longitudinal cutaway of a myelinated neuron showing the unmyelinated proximal axon segment, myelin segments separated by nodes of Ranvier and containing clefts of Schmidt-Lantermann, and unmyelinated axon terminals.
items.rn: Nerve fibre classification, conduction and degeneration

items.t: Neuromuscular junction: end plate, myasthenia and blockers
items.c: Ca2+ in, ACh out, nicotinic receptors open, end plate potential, muscle action potential, acetylcholinesterase ends the signal.
items.a: Steps at the neuromuscular junction: motor nerve action potential opens calcium channels, vesicles release acetylcholine, it binds nicotinic receptors producing an end plate potential, sodium entry fires a muscle action potential, and acetylcholinesterase removes the transmitter.
items.rn: Neuromuscular junction: end plate, myasthenia and blockers

items.t: Neuromuscular junction: end plate, myasthenia and blockers
items.c: Weakness worsens with use and improves with rest; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors help, and the thymus must be checked.
items.a: Pathology of myasthenia gravis: autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, MuSK or LRP4 reduce functional receptors, so repeated use causes fatigable weakness with ptosis and diplopia; edrophonium or pyridostigmine improve it; thymoma should be looked for.
items.rn: Neuromuscular junction: end plate, myasthenia and blockers

items.t: Neuromuscular junction: end plate, myasthenia and blockers
items.c: Suxamethonium: fasciculations, hyperkalaemia, malignant hyperthermia trigger. Rocuronium: reversed by sugammadex.
items.a: Table comparing depolarising and non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers: suxamethonium acts as an agonist causing fasciculation and hyperkalaemia and triggers malignant hyperthermia, whereas rocuronium and atracurium compete at the receptor and are reversed by neostigmine or sugammadex.
items.rn: Neuromuscular junction: end plate, myasthenia and blockers

items.t: Pain and temperature: nociceptors, fibres, and modulation
items.c: Pain and temperature cross at the spinal level within a segment or two; dorsal column modalities cross in the medulla.
items.a: Pain pathway: nociceptors with A delta and C fibres enter the dorsal horn, synapse in laminae I and II, cross in the anterior white commissure, ascend in the contralateral spinothalamic tract to the VPL thalamus and then to the somatosensory cortex; collaterals reach the periaqueductal grey and limbic system.
items.rn: Pain and temperature: nociceptors, fibres, and modulation

items.t: Pancreatic exocrine and endocrine physiology and glucose homeostasis
items.c: Secretin raises cAMP, opens CFTR, and the duct secretes bicarbonate; cystic fibrosis blocks this and thickens secretions.
items.a: Pancreatic duct cell: carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate inside, a chloride bicarbonate exchanger and CFTR chloride channel at the apical membrane secrete bicarbonate into the lumen, basolateral sodium hydrogen exchange and the sodium potassium pump support it, and secretin acts through cAMP to open CFTR.
items.rn: Pancreatic exocrine and endocrine physiology and glucose homeostasis

items.t: Pancreatic exocrine and endocrine physiology and glucose homeostasis
items.c: Histological schematic comparing exocrine acinar ductal units with endocrine islets of Langerhans, highlighting insulin secretion cascades.
items.a: Pancreatic acinar and islet histology
items.rn: Pancreatic exocrine and endocrine physiology and glucose homeostasis

items.t: Pregnancy, parturition and lactation: key hormones and physiology
items.c: Oestrogen: ducts. Progesterone: alveoli. Prolactin: milk synthesis. Oxytocin: let-down.
items.a: Table of hormones driving breast development and lactation: oestrogen grows the ducts, progesterone grows alveoli, human placental lactogen and prolactin prepare the gland, oxytocin releases milk, and high oestrogen and progesterone block milk secretion until delivery.
items.rn: Pregnancy, parturition and lactation: key hormones and physiology

items.t: Pregnancy, parturition and lactation: key hormones and physiology
items.c: Labour is a positive feedback loop, ended only by delivery; oestrogen sensitises the uterus to oxytocin.
items.a: Positive feedback loop of labour: fetal head stretches the cervix, afferent signals reach hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, the posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, uterine contractions push the head harder against the cervix, until delivery ends the loop.
items.rn: Pregnancy, parturition and lactation: key hormones and physiology

items.t: Plasma proteins, red cells and haemoglobin: core physiology for NEET-PG and USMLE
items.c: Biconcave shape gives a high surface to volume ratio and flexibility; HbA is two alpha and two beta chains, each with one haem.
items.a: Biconcave red cell in cross-section with diameter about 7.5 micrometres, and a haemoglobin molecule of two alpha and two beta chains each with a haem iron; adult HbA is alpha two beta two, HbF alpha two gamma two, HbA2 alpha two delta two.
items.rn: Plasma proteins, red cells and haemoglobin: core physiology for NEET-PG and USMLE

items.c: Tachycardia hurts twice: demand rises and diastole, when the left ventricle is perfused, shortens.
items.a: Balance of myocardial oxygen: demand rises with heart rate, contractility, wall tension from preload and afterload; supply depends on diastolic aortic pressure, coronary vascular resistance, diastolic time and oxygen content; extraction is already about 70 percent so extra demand must be met by flow.
items.rn: Regional circulation, shock and exercise

items.c: Standing pools blood in the legs; the baroreflex restores pressure within seconds.
items.a: Response to standing: 300 to 500 mL of blood pools in the leg veins, venous return and cardiac output fall, baroreceptor unloading raises sympathetic tone and lowers vagal tone, heart rate and vasoconstriction restore pressure; failure causes orthostatic hypotension.
items.rn: Regional circulation, shock and exercise

items.t: Regulation of respiration: centres, chemoreceptors and reflexes
items.c: CO2 is the main drive to breathe: ventilation climbs linearly with PaCO2, and low oxygen makes the response steeper.
items.a: Plot of ventilation against arterial PCO2: ventilation rises roughly linearly above a PCO2 of about 40 mmHg, hypoxia steepens the slope, and very high PCO2 depresses breathing.
items.rn: Regulation of respiration: centres, chemoreceptors and reflexes

items.t: Gastric acid secretion, parietal cell physiology and regulatory peptides
items.c: Histamine, gastrin and acetylcholine all converge on the proton pump; omeprazole blocks the pump itself.
items.a: Parietal cell: carbonic anhydrase makes hydrogen and bicarbonate, the apical H+ K+ ATPase pumps hydrogen into the lumen for potassium, K+ and Cl- channels supply the ions, a basolateral Cl- HCO3- exchanger sends bicarbonate to blood (alkaline tide); acetylcholine, gastrin and histamine stimulate and proton pump inhibitors block the pump.
items.rn: Gastric acid secretion, parietal cell physiology and regulatory peptides

items.c: Dorsal column: ipsilateral until the medulla. Spinothalamic: crosses at once. A cord hemisection gives mixed sides.
items.a: Two ascending sensory pathways: dorsal column medial lemniscus carrying fine touch and proprioception, ipsilateral in the cord, crossing in the medulla; spinothalamic carrying pain and temperature, crossing within the cord; both reach VPL thalamus and the postcentral gyrus.
items.rn: Sensory receptors and somatosensory pathways

items.t: Skeletal muscle contraction: coupling, cross-bridges and energy
items.c: Maximum active force at optimal overlap; too short or too long reduces force; passive tension from titin and connective tissue rises on stretch.
items.a: Length tension curves of skeletal muscle: active tension peaks at an optimal sarcomere length of about 2.0 to 2.2 micrometres where filament overlap is maximal and falls at shorter and longer lengths, while passive tension rises steeply when stretched beyond that.
items.rn: Skeletal muscle contraction: coupling, cross-bridges and energy

items.t: Smooth and cardiac muscle: key physiology for NEET-PG and USMLE
items.c: Slow waves set the rhythm; only the spikes on top of them, when threshold is crossed, produce contraction.
items.a: Trace of single unit smooth muscle membrane potential with slow waves oscillating between about minus 65 and minus 45 millivolts; action potential spikes occur on the crests when the threshold is crossed and these trigger contraction.
items.rn: Smooth and cardiac muscle: key physiology for NEET-PG and USMLE

items.t: Smooth and cardiac muscle: key physiology for NEET-PG and USMLE
items.c: Beta-1 stimulation speeds relaxation (lusitropy) and strengthens contraction through phospholamban and SERCA.
items.a: Phospholamban regulation of the cardiac sarcoplasmic reticulum: beta-1 stimulation raises cAMP and protein kinase A, which phosphorylates phospholamban, relieving its inhibition of the SERCA calcium pump, so calcium is taken up faster for quicker relaxation and larger stores for stronger contraction.
items.rn: Smooth and cardiac muscle: key physiology for NEET-PG and USMLE

items.t: Taste and smell: receptors, pathways and clinical losses
items.c: Smell reaches cortex without passing the thalamus first; taste goes via the solitary nucleus and VPM.
items.a: Table comparing taste and smell pathways: taste buds via facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the nucleus of the solitary tract, VPM thalamus and insula; olfactory neurons to the olfactory bulb glomeruli, mitral cells, olfactory tract to piriform cortex and amygdala without a thalamic relay first.
items.rn: Taste and smell: receptors, pathways and clinical losses

items.t: Taste and smell: receptors, pathways and clinical losses
items.c: Anterior two thirds: chorda tympani (VII). Posterior third including circumvallate: glossopharyngeal (IX). Filiform papillae have no taste buds.
items.a: Top view of the tongue showing the V of circumvallate papillae at the back, foliate papillae on the posterior sides, fungiform papillae over the tip and sides, and filiform papillae over the surface without taste buds, with the cranial nerve for each region.
items.rn: Taste and smell: receptors, pathways and clinical losses

items.c: Trap, oxidise, organify, couple, store, then endocytose and release; thyroid peroxidase is the target of carbimazole.
items.a: Steps of thyroid hormone synthesis: iodide trapping by the sodium iodide symporter, oxidation and organification by thyroid peroxidase onto thyroglobulin, coupling of MIT and DIT into T3 and T4 in colloid, then endocytosis and proteolysis releasing T4 and T3.
items.rn: Thyroid hormones

items.c: Thyroid hormone raises metabolism, heat, heart rate and gut motility; in infancy it is essential for brain development.
items.a: Table of thyroid hormone actions by system: raises basal metabolic rate and heat production, upregulates beta receptors, essential for fetal and childhood brain and bone growth, speeds gut motility.
items.rn: Thyroid hormones

items.c: Graves disease: TSH receptor stimulating antibodies; only Graves has eye disease and pretibial myxoedema.
items.a: Table of Graves disease features: thyroid stimulating antibodies, eye signs of lid lag and exophthalmos, pretibial myxoedema, thyroid storm with fever and agitation, and carbimazole or propylthiouracil treatment.
items.rn: Thyroid hormones

items.c: Read TSH first: high TSH with low T4 is primary hypothyroidism; low TSH with high T4 is primary hyperthyroidism.
items.a: Table of thyroid function test patterns: primary hypothyroidism high TSH low free T4, subclinical high TSH normal T4, secondary hypothyroidism low or normal TSH low T4, Graves disease low TSH high T4, rare TSH producing adenoma high TSH high T4.
items.rn: Thyroid hormones

items.t: Renal tubular transport, reabsorption and secretion mechanisms
items.c: NKCC2 is the loop diuretic target; the lumen-positive voltage drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption, which diuretics lose.
items.a: Thick ascending limb cell: NKCC2 on the apical membrane brings sodium potassium and two chloride in, ROMK returns potassium to the lumen creating a lumen positive voltage, the basolateral sodium potassium pump and chloride channel complete transport, and the positive voltage pushes calcium and magnesium through the paracellular path; the segment is water impermeable and loop diuretics block NKCC2.
items.rn: Renal tubular transport, reabsorption and secretion mechanisms

items.t: Renal tubular transport, reabsorption and secretion mechanisms
items.c: Cellular schematics detailing cotransporter, exchanger and ion channel distributions along proximal, loop and collecting duct epithelia.
items.a: Nephron tubular transport and ion channels
items.rn: Renal tubular transport, reabsorption and secretion mechanisms

items.c: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas: neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, basophil in descending order of abundance.
items.a: Table of white cell types with typical share and role: neutrophils about 60 percent for first response, lymphocytes about 30 percent adaptive immunity, monocytes becoming macrophages, eosinophils for parasites and allergy, basophils with histamine and heparin.
items.rn: WBCs, phagocytosis and innate immunity

items.c: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide; myeloperoxidase makes bleach. CGD lacks the first enzyme and fails the NBT or DHR test.
items.a: Steps of phagocytosis: chemotaxis and margination, opsonisation by C3b and IgG, engulfment into a phagosome, fusion with lysosome, oxidative burst by NADPH oxidase with myeloperoxidase making hypochlorous acid; chronic granulomatous disease lacks NADPH oxidase.
items.rn: WBCs, phagocytosis and innate immunity

items.c: Three entry pathways, one common result: opsonisation (C3b), inflammation (C3a, C5a), lysis (MAC C5b-9).
items.a: Complement activation: classical pathway by C1 on antibody, alternative pathway by spontaneous C3b on microbes, lectin pathway by mannose binding lectin, all forming C3 convertase and then C5 convertase; C3b opsonises, C3a and C5a recruit cells, C5b to C9 form the membrane attack complex.
items.rn: WBCs, phagocytosis and innate immunity
